name: Necrotizing Fasciitis

veryLikely: Streptococcus pyogenes (Group A Streptococcus) - monomicrobial type II
Polymicrobial flora including anaerobes and Enterobacteriaceae - type I (more common, often in diabetics/immunocompromised)
pathogens.why: Necrotizing fasciitis is classified as type I (polymicrobial, typically in diabetics or after abdominal surgery) or type II (monomicrobial, classically Group A Streptococcus, can occur in healthy individuals). Empiric coverage must be broad enough to address both patterns until surgical/microbiological findings narrow the picture.

investigations.why: The definitive diagnostic test - direct visualization of necrotic fascia confirms the diagnosis and simultaneously allows debridement; imaging should not delay surgery when clinical suspicion is high.

investigations.test: Blood cultures and intraoperative tissue/fluid cultures
investigations.why: Identifies the causative organism(s) to guide de-escalation.

investigations.test: CT or MRI (only if diagnosis uncertain and patient stable enough to tolerate delay)
investigations.why: May show fascial thickening/gas, but should never delay surgery in a patient with high clinical suspicion.
Markedly elevated levels suggest muscle involvement (myonecrosis), affecting the extent of surgical debridement needed.

investigations.test: LRINEC score (Laboratory Risk Indicator for Necrotizing Fasciitis)
investigations.why: Can support clinical suspicion using CRP, WBC, hemoglobin, sodium, creatinine, and glucose, though it should not override strong clinical suspicion if score is low.

references: IDSA Skin and Soft Tissue Infection Guidelines
reason: pain out of proportion to examination findings

raise urgent concern for necrotizing fasciitis - a surgical emergency where mortality rises sharply with every hour of delay. EMERGENT surgical consultation for exploration and debridement must happen in parallel with antibiotics, not after - antibiotics alone do not cure necrotizing soft tissue infection.

clinicalPearls: Pain out of proportion to physical findings is the classic early clue: physical signs may be minimal (only soft-tissue edema and mild erythema) while pain and fever are severe; this disparity helps distinguish NF from superficial cellulitis, where skin appearance is more abnormal but pain is only mild-to-moderate.

Early disease is frequently misdiagnosed (e.g., as thrombophlebitis) and patients may be sent home with analgesics, especially in the strep type that begins deep at a site of non-penetrating minor trauma (bruise, muscle strain) with no visible portal of entry.

Classic late signs evolve sequentially: swelling and brawny edema/tenderness, then dark-red (violaceous) induration, then bullae filled with blue/purple fluid, then friable bluish-maroon-to-black skin; thrombosis of dermal-papillae vessels is extensive by this stage.
Paradoxical decrease in pain or progression to anesthesia over the involved area is an ominous sign reflecting thrombosis of small vessels and infarction of cutaneous nerves.
GAS NF can be preceded by varicella, childbirth, or muscle strain, and most patients deny an antecedent streptococcal infection.
The inoculation site may be inapparent and remote from clinical involvement (e.g., minor hand trauma manifesting as infection over the shoulder or chest).
Myositis/myonecrosis coexists with NF in roughly 20-50% of cases and serum creatine phosphokinase (CPK) may be markedly elevated, signaling deeper muscle involvement.
harrison.pathophysiology: NF is infection of the superficial and/or deep fascia investing the muscles of an extremity or trunk, with extensive necrosis of subcutaneous tissue and fascia. Infection spreads rapidly along fascial planes and via venous channels and lymphatics, typically sparing the muscle itself in pure fasciitis. Two main microbiologic patterns: a mixed aerobic-anaerobic (type I) process beginning with a breach of a mucosal barrier (GI/GU tract), and a monomicrobial group A streptococcal (type II) process. In GAS disease, organisms reach deep fascia either by transient bacteremic seeding at a site of minor non-penetrating trauma (no portal) or by spread from cutaneous infection/penetrating trauma. Thrombosis of dermal vessels produces progressive skin necrosis; infarction of cutaneous nerves causes the characteristic late anesthesia. NF caused by Clostridium perfringens or extending into muscle (clostridial/streptococcal myonecrosis) carries very high systemic toxicity with hemolysis. PVL-producing MRSA strains have been reported as a cause.
additionalDifferentials: Clostridial myonecrosis / gas gangrene (distinguished from clostridial NF by muscle biopsy)
Streptococcal necrotizing myositis (GAS infection extending into muscle)
Pyomyositis (usually S. aureus; localized, shock uncommon unless toxin-producing)
Synergistic nonclostridial anaerobic myonecrosis (necrotizing cutaneous myositis / synergistic necrotizing cellulitis) - a mixed aerobic-anaerobic variant
Cellulitis / erysipelas (superficial; skin more abnormal but pain mild-moderate)
Halophilic Vibrio vulnificus infection (can be as fulminant as NF; Gulf/Atlantic water exposure or raw seafood in cirrhosis)
infectionMimics: Aggressive cellulitis from Vibrio vulnificus or Aeromonas hydrophila
nonInfectiousMimics: Muscle strain or contusion (the minor trauma at the deep nidus)
additionalInvestigations: Soft-tissue plain radiography, CT, and MRI to assess depth of infection and detect tissue gas or a localized abscess - most useful when lesions progress rapidly or SIRS is present; note imaging may show only soft-tissue swelling and is NOT specific for fulminant GAS NF/myonecrosis, where gas is typically absent
Gram stain and aerobic/anaerobic culture of surgically excised tissue to identify GAS vs mixed flora vs MRSA vs Clostridium
Frozen-section histology of aspirate or punch biopsy (valuable in NF), though aspiration/biopsy is negative in ~80% of cases
Serum CPK (markedly elevated when myonecrosis coexists)
Lactate, d-dimer, coagulation, liver and renal function as markers of systemic toxicity/organ failure
redFlags: Pain out of proportion to examination findings
Rapidly progressing lesion with signs of systemic inflammatory response / toxicity
Violaceous (blue/purple) bullae, skin sloughing, dusky/mottled erythema
Progression of tenderness to anesthesia over the lesion (cutaneous nerve infarction)
Crepitus or gas in deep tissue (suggests mixed/clostridial infection)
Renal impairment that may precede shock, plus hypotension/multiorgan failure
Urgent surgical exploration supersedes other diagnostic or therapeutic maneuvers - debridement is life-saving and must not be delayed
harrison.prognosis: Mortality for NF is roughly 11-34% overall and rises substantially when associated with toxic shock syndrome. GAS/clostridial fascial-muscle infection historically carried 20-50% mortality with penicillin alone. Survivors of GAS NF often require repeated surgeries including amputation. Clostridial NF/myonecrosis is far more lethal: spontaneous (nontraumatic) myonecrosis mortality exceeds 65% (often C. septicum with underlying malignancy); trunk infection ~63% vs limb ~12% mortality. Any delay in surgery increases the risk of death; early aggressive surgery markedly improves outcomes.
pitfalls: Early physical findings are minimal relative to pain/fever, leading to underestimation of severity and misdiagnosis as thrombophlebitis or simple cellulitis.
Absence of gas does NOT exclude NF: gas is usually absent when the cause is GAS or MRSA and is seen mainly with mixed/clostridial infection.
Normal or nonspecific imaging does NOT rule out NF - CT/MRI may show only soft-tissue swelling and are not specific for fulminant GAS NF/myonecrosis.
A negative aspirate or frozen-section biopsy does NOT exclude NF (negative in ~80% of cases).
Decreasing pain should not be reassuring - it can signal nerve infarction and disease progression rather than improvement.
Do not wait for imaging or cultures when NF is suspected with systemic toxicity; surgical exploration is both diagnostic and therapeutic.
harrison.severityClassification: Microbiologic/clinical typing: Type I = mixed aerobic-anaerobic, begins at a mucosal-barrier breach (GI/GU), common in diabetes, peripheral vascular disease, malignancy, surgery, or abdominal penetrating injury; Fournier gangrene is the perineal/scrotal form. Type II = monomicrobial group A streptococcal (GAS implicated in ~60% of NF cases), can occur in otherwise healthy hosts, two presentations (with vs without a defined portal of entry). PVL-producing MRSA is a recognized monomicrobial cause. NF qualifies as soft-tissue necrosis under the CDC streptococcal toxic shock syndrome case definition (hypotension plus >=2 of: renal impairment, coagulopathy, hepatic impairment, ARDS, generalized erythematous desquamating rash, soft-tissue necrosis/NF/myositis/gangrene). (LRINEC score not described in this source.)
